KEEP THE LOGIC. SKIP THE GUESSWORK.

Your subnetting field notes.

The few rules that make all the questions work.

01 / THE CORE RULE

The slash fixes the first bits.

IPv4 has 32 bits. In /27, the first 27 stay the same for every address in that subnet. The last 5 bits vary from 00000 to 11111.

32 − prefix = host bits
2host bits = total addresses
total − 2 = usable hosts

A /27 has 32 addresses. It does not mean 27 hosts, and it does not always start at .0.

02 / THE ENDPOINTS

Zeroes first. Ones last.

  • Network: set every host bit to 0; IP AND mask.
  • Broadcast: set every host bit to 1; network + size − 1.
  • First usable: network + 1.
  • Last usable: broadcast − 1.

A /24 spans the whole last octet, .0–.255. A /27 spans an aligned 32-address block: .0–.31, .32–.63, .64–.95, and so on.

03 / COMMON PREFIXES

Useful numbers to recognize

PrefixMaskAddressesUsable
04 / CLASS B & VARIABLE RANGES

Let the boundary do the work.

Class B exercise: start at /16. Four equal subnets need log₂4 = 2 borrowed bits, giving /18. The third mask octet is 11000000₂ = 192, so the mask is 255.255.192.0.

Range counting: end − start + 1, using the full 32-bit values. A power-of-two count must also start at an aligned boundary to be one CIDR block.

VLSM: allocate largest requests first. Choose the smallest power of two ≥ hosts + 2, then use the next aligned network boundary.

In modern CIDR routing, use the given prefix; do not infer the mask from the first octet.
